name: Diosmin
lead: Diosmin is a citrus-derived flavonoid (diosmetin 7-O-rutinoside) used as a venoactive, or phlebotonic, agent. People take it for the look and comfort of their legs and for swelling and bruising: it is used in chronic venous disease, which includes leg swelling, heaviness, spider and varicose veins, and in post-injury or post-surgery swelling, and it appears in bruise-support supplements [1][2][3].

It is usually taken orally, often as a micronised purified flavonoid fraction of 90% diosmin and 10% hesperidin sold in Europe as Daflon or Detralex, whereas in the US it is sold as a dietary supplement and a standardised micronised product, Vasculera [2][3]. It is made commercially from hesperidin extracted from citrus peel and was first isolated in 1925 [1][3].

Reviews describe the venoactive class as sealing the endothelial barrier, enhancing lymphatic drainage, improving venous tone and reducing leukocyte adhesion, and a 2025 review gave micronised purified flavonoid fraction among the highest-quality evidence in its field for symptoms and swelling [4][5]. A randomized trial of 330 knee-replacement patients and smaller studies have reported reduced swelling with diosmin [6][7].

For appearance goals, diosmin is of interest where swelling, puffiness and bruising change how a body part looks, and where recovery from exercise is a factor. No trial has tested it for facial puffiness or other cosmetic outcomes [1][2][8].

Less fluid leaks into surrounding tissue; lymph drainage improves
Reduced swelling and heaviness in the legs and ankles
Slimmer, less puffy look and smoother recovery after injury or surgery
angle.text: Diosmin is taken to reduce swelling and the look of tired, swollen legs, and it features in bruise-support formulas alongside arnica, bromelain and vitamin C. Trials have measured limb circumference and swelling after surgery or injury rather than face puffiness [2][6][7].

paras: People associate diosmin with slimmer, less swollen legs and ankles, less visible leg veins and faster fading of bruises. Over-the-counter bruise formulas such as one listed in the US DailyMed database combine diosmin with arnica, bromelain, rutin, citrus bioflavonoids, hesperidin methyl chalcone, vitamin C and zinc and say they support recovery from bruising after minor injuries or surgery [2].

A 2025 systematic review of swelling management after total knee replacement named diosmin among the adjunctive therapies that showed promise, alongside acupuncture and kinesiotaping [8]. In looksmaxxing contexts it is of interest for puffiness and swelling in general, though studies have concerned the legs rather than the face [8][6].

The established use is symptomatic treatment of chronic venous disease, haemorrhoids and leg swelling. Wikipedia rates the evidence as moderate for leg and ankle swelling and lower-leg pain and lower for haemorrhoids, and notes that some professional societies mention phlebotonics as an option for mild haemorrhoids [3]. A 2025 review of venoactive compounds assessed symptom relief for pain, cramps and heaviness and reduction of oedema, with micronised purified flavonoid fraction showing the highest-quality evidence, and listed it as an adjunct for venous leg ulcers [5].

After oral intake diosmin is converted to its aglycone diosmetin, which is absorbed, esterified into glucuronide conjugates and excreted in urine [9]. Reviews report that it prolongs noradrenaline-induced venous constriction, reduces capillary permeability and leukocyte adhesion, and has anti-inflammatory and antioxidant effects [1][4][9]. Venoactive compounds as a class are described as sealing the endothelial barrier, enhancing lymphatic drainage, improving venous tone and lowering blood viscosity [5].

A 2003 screen examined diosmin and other flavonoids at the aryl hydrocarbon receptor, and a 2022 pharmacology review noted inhibitory effects on several metabolic enzymes, a reason it suggests considering drug interactions [9][10].
Diosmin is a flavone glycoside, the rutinoside of diosmetin. It is prepared semisynthetically from hesperidin, a flavanone abundant in citrus peel [1][3][9].

Grokipedia reports symptom improvements of up to about 50% in leg heaviness, pain and oedema over two to six months with micronised purified flavonoid fraction, a secondary statement that has not been verified against primary papers [1].

In a 2024 randomized, controlled multicentre trial in 13 university-affiliated tertiary hospitals, 330 patients undergoing knee replacement received 0.9 g of diosmin twice daily for 14 days or no treatment. Diosmin was associated with significantly less calf, thigh and patellar swelling at every time point and lower pain on movement, with no differences in rest pain, knee scores, inflammatory markers or complications [6].

A 2023 randomized trial of 60 outpatients with persistent ankle oedema after fractures or sprains tested a product combining diosmin, coumarin and arbutin for six weeks on top of conventional care; ankle circumference improved by about 4 to 5% more in the product group and function scores improved [7].

A 2025 crossover trial in 15 professional female futsal players tested 750 mg of diosmin daily for three days against placebo around an intense lower-limb protocol. Diosmin did not change athletic performance; some soreness, oxidative stress, strength and balance measures showed trivial-to-moderate effect sizes that were not statistically significant, which the authors read as suggesting a possible benefit [11]. In a 2022 Russian trial of spa therapy for post-thrombophlebitic syndrome, the comparison group used compression with a diosmin-hesperidin combination [12].

Product labels for bruise formulas containing diosmin list mild gastrointestinal upset and rash, and rarely prolonged bleeding or hypersensitivity [2]. Wikipedia reports that roughly 10% of users may have mild digestive or skin reactions, that it is not recommended for children or during pregnancy, and that the FDA concluded in 2001 that evidence on safety was inadequate for a prescription application [3]. A 2022 review judged the toxicological profile favourable while recommending attention to interactions with drugs metabolised by inhibited enzymes [9].

Animal and early studies have reported that diosmin protects against ethanol-induced gastric injury and chemically induced colon carcinogenesis in rats, and reduces gentamicin-induced kidney damage and experimental renal fibrosis [13][14][15][16]. Registered trials examine diosmin or diosmin-hesperidin in ovarian hyperstimulation prevention, ulcerative colitis, fatty liver disease, peptic ulcer, chemotherapy-related bone pain and neuropathy, scleroderma digital ulcers and post-surgical seroma [17][18][19][20][21].

Published randomized trials include the 330-patient knee replacement study (2024), the 60-patient ankle oedema study (2023) and the 15-athlete soreness trial (2025) described above [6][7][11]. A 120-person phase 4 trial compared diosmin 600 mg with diosmin plus hesperidin in symptomatic chronic venous insufficiency [22]. Further registered studies in other conditions are listed under Research [17][18][19][20][21].
No studies found on facial puffiness, under-eye swelling or other cosmetic uses.

Diosmin was first isolated in 1925 [1]. Wikipedia notes US regulatory milestones in 2001 and 2013 and a 2017 recommendation from the American Working Group in Chronic Venous Disease [3]. Availability varies by country: prescription or over-the-counter in parts of Europe, restricted in Spain to chronic venous disease, not approved in Germany, and sold as a supplement in the US [3].

card.summary: A citrus flavonoid used for leg-vein swelling; interest for face puffiness is untested.
card.note: Prescription in parts of Europe; no cosmetic trials found.

quick.overview:
Diosmin is a citrus flavonoid used to treat chronic venous insufficiency and haemorrhoids, usually with hesperidin. It is a prescription medicine in parts of Europe and a supplement in the US.

It is listed in bruise and swelling supplements; use for facial puffiness has not been tested.
quick.mechanism: It is reported to raise venous tone, reduce capillary permeability and dampen leukocyte-driven inflammation after conversion to diosmetin.
quick.risks: Product labels mention mild stomach upset, nausea and rash, rarely bleeding or hypersensitivity. Combination bruise products carry additional warnings for their other ingredients.
